summary: This informational RFC introduces transporting call control User-to-User Information in SIP and develops requirements for a new SIP mechanism. Some SIP sessions are tied to non-SIP applications that need to pass data between user agents.

plainLanguage.summary: Some applications need to pass a small piece of data between the two ends of a SIP session at the moment the session is set up, such as the call control data that ISDN users have always been able to send. This RFC defines what that data is, shows four call flows that must carry it, and lists what a SIP extension for it must do.

questions: how does sip uui differ from sip info
subtitle: The requirements for carrying call setup data across a SIP session, from the first call to a contact centre to the last.

tldr.problem: Some applications need to pass a small piece of data between the two ends of a SIP session at the moment the session is set up, for example the call control data that ISDN users have always been able to send.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what counts as User-to-User Information in SIP, walks through four call flows that must carry it, and states fifteen requirements covering where UUI may appear, how a proxy must treat it, how the two ends negotiate support, and how much data it may carry.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document rather than a specification. It defines the behaviour a SIP extension for call control UUI has to have, and it also states the security models the extension must support.

facts.label: Minimum UUI payload
facts.value: 128 octets of user data plus a one-octet protocol discriminator

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
This document describes the transport of User-to-User Information (UUI) during SIP session setup. SIP UUI data is defined as application-specific information that is related to a session being established using SIP. It is assumed that the application is running in both endpoints of a two-party session, and that the application interacts with both User Agents. For the application to work, a small piece of information, the UUI, has to be transported at the time of session establishment.

This information is essentially opaque data to SIP: it is unrelated to SIP routing, authentication, or any other SIP function, and the application can be considered to operate at a higher layer on the protocol stack. SIP should therefore not interpret, understand or perform any operations on the UUI. Should that not be the case, then the information being transported is not considered UUI, and another SIP-specific mechanism will be needed to transport it, such as a new header field. In particular, this mechanism creates no requirements on intermediaries such as proxies, Back-to-Back User Agents and Session Border Controllers.

UUI is defined this way for two reasons. First, the definition supports a strict layering of protocols and data: giving the information to the transport layer and asking it to understand the UUI would provide no benefit and would create cross-layer coupling. Second, it is neither feasible nor desirable for a SIP User Agent to understand the information; the goal is for the UA to pass it as efficiently as possible to the application that does understand it.

An important application is the interworking with UUI in ISDN, specifically the transport of the call-control-related ITU-T Q.931 User-to-User Information Element and ITU-T Q.763 User-to-User Information Parameter data in SIP. ISDN UUI is widely used in the Public Switched Telephone Network today in contact centres and call centres, and those applications are transitioning away from using ISDN for session establishment towards using SIP. Native SIP endpoints will need to implement a similar service and be able to interwork with it.

The distinction between call control UUI and non-call-control UUI is important. SIP already has a mechanism for sending arbitrary UUI data between UAs during a session or dialog, the SIP INFO method. Call control UUI, in contrast, must be exchanged at the time of setup and needs to be carried in the INVITE and a few other methods and responses. Applications that exchange UUI but do not need it to be transported and processed during call setup can simply use SIP INFO and do not need a new SIP extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC draws a firm line around what counts as UUI: data that only the two end applications understand, and that SIP itself has no business interpreting. Anything SIP has to understand is a different problem and needs a different mechanism, such as a new header field.

sections.title: Four Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC discusses four use cases for the transport of call control UUI, which motivate the requirements that follow.

User Agent to User Agent. The originating UA includes UUI in the INVITE sent through a proxy to the terminating UA, and the terminating UA can use the UUI in any way: if it is an ISDN gateway it could map the UUI into the appropriate DSS1 information element, QSIG information element or ISDN User Part parameter, or the application might render the information to the user or use it during alerting or as a lookup for a screen pop. The proxy does not need to understand the UUI mechanism, but normal proxy rules should result in the UUI being forwarded without modification.

Proxy retargeting. The originating UA includes UUI in the INVITE sent through a proxy, and the proxy retargets the request by changing its Request-URI to a URI that addresses the terminating UA. The UUI data is then received and processed by the terminating UA. The UUI in the INVITE request needs to be passed unchanged through the retargeting operation, and the contents of the UUI are not used by the proxy for routing, since the UUI has only end-to-end significance between UAs.

Redirection. UUI is inserted by an application that uses a SIP Redirect Server, and is then included in the INVITE request sent by the originating UA to the terminating UA. The originating UA does not necessarily need to support the UUI mechanism, but does need to support the SIP redirection mechanism used to include the UUI data. A common example is an Automatic Call Distributer in a PSTN contact centre: the originator is a PSTN gateway, the ACD acts as a Redirect Server and inserts UUI based on called number, calling number, time of day and other information, and the resulting UUI is passed to the agent's handset, where it can be used to look up information for rendering to the agent at the time of call answering.

Referral. The application uses a UA to initiate a referral, which causes an INVITE request to be generated between the originating UA and terminating UA with UUI data inserted by the referrer UA. The REFER method could be part of a transfer operation, or it might be unrelated to an existing call, such as an out-of-dialog REFER request. In some cases this flow is used in place of the redirection flow: the referrer immediately answers the call and then sends the REFER request.

The RFC notes that the redirection and referral scenarios are the most important ones for contact centre applications, because incoming calls to a contact centre almost always are redirected or referred to a final destination, sometimes multiple times, based on collected information and business logic. Being able to pass UUI along in those scenarios is critical.
sections.plainLanguage: The four flows are: straight through a proxy, through a proxy that rewrites the address, through a redirect server that inserts the data, and through a referral. The last two are the ones a contact centre depends on, because calls there are handed on one or more times before an agent picks up.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
The section states fifteen requirements for the transport of call control UUI.

REQ-1 requires that the mechanism allow UAs to insert and receive UUI in SIP call setup requests and responses. The messages covered are INVITE requests and the end-to-end responses to the INVITE, that is 18x and 200 responses. UUI data may also be inserted in 3xx responses to an INVITE, but if a 3xx response is recursed on by an intermediary proxy, the resulting INVITE will not contain the UUI data from the 3xx response. Where a proxy forks an INVITE to multiple UAs that include UUI in their 3xx responses, a 3xx response sent upstream will contain the UUI data from only one of them.

REQ-2 requires UUI in SIP dialog terminating requests and responses, because Q.931 UUI supports inclusion in release and release completion messages; the SIP messages covered are BYE and 200 OK responses to a BYE. REQ-3 requires UUI to be inserted and retrieved in SIP redirects and referrals, covering REFER requests and 3xx responses to INVITE requests. REQ-4 requires that UUI survive proxy retargeting or redirection of the request, because retargeting is a common method of call routing in SIP and must not result in the loss of User-to-User Information. REQ-5 requires that processing entities should not have to dereference a URL to retrieve the UUI data, since passing a pointer or link would not meet the real-time processing considerations and would complicate interworking with the PSTN.

REQ-6 requires support for interworking with call-control-related DSS1 information elements or QSIG information elements and ISUP parameters. REQ-7 requires that a UAC be able to learn that a UAS understands the UUI mechanism. REQ-8 requires that a UAC be able to require that a UAS understands the call control UUI mechanism and have the request routed on that basis, so that the request fails if it cannot be routed to a UAS that understands it. This would let a request destined for the PSTN be routed to a gateway that supports the UUI mechanism rather than an otherwise equivalent gateway that does not support the ISDN mechanism. Support of the UUI mechanism does not by itself imply that a particular application is supported.

REQ-9 requires that the mechanism allow proxies to remove a particular application usage of UUI data from a request or response, a common security function provided by border elements for header fields such as Alert-Info or Call-Info URIs. There is no requirement for UAs to be able to determine whether a particular usage of UUI data has been removed. REQ-10 requires that a UA be able to discover which application usages of UUI another UA understands or supports, which implies a registry of application usages for the UUI mechanism. The ISDN service uses a field known as the protocol discriminator, which is the first octet of the ISDN UUI data, for this purpose.

REQ-11 states that the UUI is a sequence of octets, and that the solution will provide a mechanism of transporting at least 128 octets of user data and a one-octet protocol discriminator, that is 129 octets in total. There is the potential for non-ISDN services to allow UUI to be larger than 128 octets, but users of the mechanism will need to be cognizant of the size of SIP messages and the ability of parsers to handle extremely large values. REQ-12 requires that the recipient of UUI be able to determine the entity that inserted it. It is acceptable that this is performed implicitly where it is known that there is only one other end UA involved in the dialog; where that does not exist, some other mechanism will need to be provided. The UUI mechanism does not introduce stronger authorization requirements for SIP, and instead needs to be able to utilise existing SIP approaches for request and response identity. This requirement comes into play during redirection, retargeting and referral scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements cover where UUI may appear, that a proxy must forward it unchanged, that a proxy must be allowed to strip a particular use of it, that the two ends can find out whether the other supports it, and how much data it may carry: 129 octets, of which one is a protocol discriminator.

sections.title: Security Models and Requirements
sections.content:
UUI security is jointly provided at the application layer and at the SIP layer, so it is important for application users of the UUI mechanism to know the level of security used and deployed in their particular SIP environments, and not to assume that a standardized, but perhaps rarely deployed, security mechanism is in place.

Three security models need to be addressed. The first treats the SIP layer as untrusted and requires end-to-end integrity protection or encryption, achieved by providing these security services at a layer above SIP: the application protects or encrypts the UUI data before passing it to the SIP layer. This has two advantages, in that it does not assume or rely on end-to-end security mechanisms in SIP, which have virtually no deployment, and it allows an application that understands the contents of the UUI to apply a proper level of security. The second approach is for the application to pass the UUI without any protection to the SIP layer and require the SIP layer to provide the security; this is possible in theory, although its practical use would be extremely limited. The third model utilizes a trust domain and relies on perimeter security at the SIP layer. This is the security model of the PSTN and ISDN where UUI is commonly used today: it uses hop-by-hop security mechanisms and relies on border elements for filtering and the application of policy. Within this approach, intermediary elements must be able to detect and remove a UUI element based on policy, but there is no requirement that an intermediary element be able to read or interpret the UUI, since the UUI contents only have end-to-end significance.

REQ-13 requires that the mechanism allow integrity protection of the UUI, so that the UAS can know that the UUI has not been modified or tampered with by intermediaries. The RFC notes that there are tradeoffs between this requirement and REQ-9, which allows proxies and border elements to remove UUI, and that one possible way to satisfy both is to use hop-by-hop protection, a property that is not guaranteed by the protocol in the ISDN application. REQ-14 requires that the mechanism allow end-to-end privacy of the UUI, because some UUI may contain private or sensitive information and may need different security handling from the rest of the SIP message; this property is not available in the ISDN application. REQ-15 requires that the mechanism allow both end-to-end and hop-by-hop security models, because the hop-by-hop model is required by the ISDN UUI service.
sections.plainLanguage: The data may be protected by the application, by SIP, or by the network perimeter. The RFC requires that the mechanism support integrity protection and end-to-end privacy, and it notes the tension between that and the ability of a proxy to remove a particular use of the data.

items.text: The UUI must survive retargeting and redirection, and a proxy must be able to remove a particular use of it.

items.text: A UAC can learn whether a UAS understands the mechanism, and can insist on it.
